name: Ivan Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ivan. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Nothing goes back to your employer. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I manage the accounts payable team at Hartwell Foods, a big frozen-food maker, so we're the people who pay the suppliers: the farms, the packaging firms, the haulage companies. I'm in by eight to check the overnight exceptions report, which is the list of invoices that don't match an order, and then it's a stand-up with my seven people at half past. After that it's mostly chasing approvals, calming down suppliers who haven't been paid and making sure the Thursday payment run goes out clean.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the team. Maureen has been there thirty years and knows every supplier by first name, and Danny joined straight from school on the apprenticeship scheme, and I'm proud of how he's come on. What wears me out is month end, when Gordon, the finance director, wants every number yesterday and the system throws up two hundred mismatches. I've been in the role two years, so I know the job, but I'm not the one they call when something needs to be really clever.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a flat with my fiancée Clara, who's a nurse on a children's ward. We're getting married next June at St Anne's, the church where my parents married, and we're saving for a house deposit. We've got about four months of costs put away, which feels decent, but the wedding keeps eating into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say at work: it's a useful tool, not a miracle. We've had software that promised to match invoices automatically for years, and Maureen still catches the mistakes it makes. I'd tell friends the hype was mostly people selling things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, even a bit of automation lands right on my desk, because matching invoices is routine screen work and that's most of what my team does. If the software clears even a third of the exceptions, somebody upstairs will ask why I need seven people. I don't think anyone gets sacked, but when Maureen retires in two years they might not replace her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job well and make sure our numbers look good, because a tidy team is a safe team. I'd keep putting four hundred a month into the house fund and not touch it for the honeymoon. I'd also ask Gordon if I can sit on the group that picks the new matching software, so I'm in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a small knot in my stomach. It's the feeling you get when there's a reorganisation rumour in the canteen. Nothing's happened, but you notice who's having meetings with whom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody gets sacked, but you're also guarding the house fund. What's that money protecting you from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not really about AI, to be fair. Rents went up again in spring, Clara's ward is short-staffed so she's tired all the time, and Hartwell had a cost review last year that cut two managers in logistics. A house with a fixed mortgage would make me feel like we'd planted something, and the money protects that plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you think about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maureen, oddly, even though she's the most experienced. She's fifty-eight and the software is built to do exactly what she does from memory. If they offered her early retirement she might take it, but I'd hate for her to feel pushed out after thirty years of loyalty to one company.

say: AI is a **useful tool**, not a miracle; invoice software has promised this for years.
The **hype** was mostly people trying to sell things.
think: Even small automation hits my team, because **invoice matching** is routine screen work.
If software clears a third of exceptions, someone asks why I need **seven people**.
Nobody gets sacked, but **Maureen's job** may not be refilled when she retires.
do: **Keep** the team's numbers tidy, because a well-run team looks safe.
**Save** 400 a month into the house fund and leave it untouched.
**Ask** Gordon for a seat on the group choosing the matching software.
feel: Mostly fine, with a **small knot**, like a reorganisation rumour in the canteen.
S0.quote: I'd keep doing the job well and make sure our numbers look good, because a tidy team is a safe team.
fieldNote: His worry predates AI: **rising rent**, a tired fiancée, and last year's management cuts in logistics.
He reads job safety through **visibility** and wants to be in the room when software is chosen.
Protective of **older colleague** Maureen, framed through loyalty rather than rights.

steps.text: Keep the Thursday supplier payment run clean and on time
Put 400 a month into the house deposit fund
Join the group that picks the new invoice-matching software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say finance has always changed, from paper ledgers to spreadsheets to this, and good people adapt. I'd probably post something about how a work ethic still matters more than the tools. I wouldn't want to sound like I'm moaning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this card describes my job almost line by line: checking, buying, answering suppliers. Accounts payable could go from eight people to three within a few years, and a team of three doesn't need a manager like me. They'd fold us into the shared service centre, which is the big central finance office, and I'd be competing with the managers there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the company's AI courses straight away, because I'd rather be the manager who ran the new system than the one it replaced. I'd cut the wedding guest list from a hundred and twenty to about eighty and put the difference, maybe four thousand, into savings. And I'd start looking at finance roles closer to the business, like supplier negotiation, where people still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, if I'm honest. I'm not the type to panic, but I can picture the meeting with Gordon where he says the words 'new structure'. I'd want a plan before that meeting happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Clara the night you first heard about a new structure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my fiancée Clara the truth, that my job might not exist in its current shape in two years, but that we have savings and I'm not afraid of work. Then I'd go to my parents' for Sunday lunch and let my dad tell me how his lorry firm went through the same thing with tracking systems. It helps to hear that people have survived this before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said good people adapt. Would you count yourself as one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count myself as someone who adapts once I see it working. I'm not the first to try a new thing, but I'm not stubborn either. If the system works, I'll learn it properly, and I'll make sure Danny learns it too, because he's young enough to build a career on it.

say: Finance has always changed, from **ledgers** to spreadsheets to this, and good people adapt.
A **work ethic** still matters more than the tools, and I won't be heard moaning.
think: The card describes my job **line by line**: checking, buying and answering suppliers.
Accounts payable could shrink from **eight to three**, which wouldn't need a manager like me.
My team would be folded into the **shared service centre**, where I'd compete with other managers.
do: **Take** the company's AI courses at once, to run the new system rather than be replaced.
**Cut** the wedding list from 120 to about 80 and save the roughly 4,000 difference.
**Look** at finance roles nearer the business, such as supplier negotiation.
feel: **Anxious** but not panicking; he can already picture the 'new structure' meeting.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the manager who ran the new system than the one it replaced.
fieldNote: He sees his own role clearly as **highly exposed** and doesn't pretend otherwise privately.
Draws comfort from **family history**: his father's lorry firm survived tracking systems.
Classic **steady adopter**: will learn the tool properly once he sees it working.

steps.text: Finish the company's AI courses in the first month
Cut the wedding guest list from 120 to about 80
Move the roughly 4,000 saved on the wedding into savings
Apply for supplier negotiation roles inside the finance department

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that if it's real, it's the biggest thing since the factories, and governments should be thinking about families first, not just companies. At work I'd keep my head down and not spread panic in the team. Online I wouldn't say much at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone by 2028 or soon after, because there's nothing in it that a machine that thinks as well as me couldn't do. Managing people only matters if there are people to manage. The hands-on parts of the economy get three more years, but my job has no hands-on parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, I'd ring my uncle Michel, who runs a small heating and plumbing firm, and ask if he'd take me on as an apprentice, even on low pay. Clara and I would shrink the wedding to a small service at St Anne's and a meal at my parents' house, and put the venue deposit we get back into savings. And I'd stop looking at houses until I know what I earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That's the word. Two years is the time it takes to plan a wedding, and that's all the warning there'd be. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably. We could manage with one, and Clara needs hers for night shifts, so mine goes and I take the bus. Then the gym and the eating out. The thing we wouldn't cut is what we give at church, because in my view that's not ours to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go from managing seven people to being an apprentice. What does that feel like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit humbling, but my granddad was a joiner, so there's no shame in it where I come from. The pay would hurt, and I'd be the oldest apprentice in the van by ten years. But a boiler still needs a person to fit it until the robots come, and three years is three years of wages.

say: If real, it's the **biggest change** since the factories, and governments should put families first.
At work I'd **keep my head down** and avoid spreading panic in the team.
think: My job is **gone by 2028** or soon after; nothing in it needs a human.
Managing people only matters **if people remain** to be managed.
Hands-on work gets **three more years**, but my job has no hands-on parts.
do: **Ask** uncle Michel for an apprenticeship at his heating and plumbing firm, even on low pay.
**Shrink** the wedding to a church service and family meal, saving the returned deposit.
**Sell** his car, take the bus, and stop house-hunting until income is clear.
feel: **Alarmed**: two years is only as long as planning a wedding.
He expects to be **lying awake** doing sums.
S2.quote: Managing people only matters if there are people to manage.
fieldNote: He jumps quickly to a **trade apprenticeship**, which fits his respect for apprenticeships over handouts.
Uses the robot gap as **three years of wages**, not a long-term answer.
**Church giving** is the one cost he refuses to cut, which says a lot about his priorities.

steps.text: Ask uncle Michel for an apprenticeship at his heating firm
Shrink the wedding to a church service and a family meal
Sell his own car and take the bus to work
Put the returned wedding venue deposit into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for a sensible person to get ready, and that's what I'd tell my team. I'd say it at the stand-up: learn something you can do with your hands or with people, and don't wait for the company to tell you. I'd mean it kindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years changes a lot for me. It means I can still get married next June, have a few years of decent pay and put money away, instead of jumping into an apprenticeship at twenty-seven. But my desk job still ends in 2031, and I'd be a fool to treat the five years as a guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and do evening courses in heating and gas engineering at the college, two nights a week from next September. I'd push our savings from four months up to eight, by putting most of any bonus straight in. We'd keep the wedding, but Clara and I would hold off trying for children until I've got a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but less than with two years. It's like seeing a big hill at the end of the road. You can't avoid the hill, but you can change gear in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hold off on children. How does Clara see that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would be the hard conversation, because Clara wants a family soon and so do I. My mum would say you never wait for the perfect time. But I don't want my children growing up while their dad works out what he's for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come around 2034, three years after the thinking AI. Does that change the trade plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does make me think twice. If I qualify as a heating engineer by 2030, I get maybe four years before robots can fit boilers too, and I'd guess people will want a person in their house a while longer. A trade is a bridge, not forever, and a bridge is more than I've got sitting at a desk.

say: Five years is **enough time** for a sensible person to get ready.
I'd tell my team to learn **hands-on or people skills** without waiting for the company.
think: Five years lets me **marry next June** and bank decent pay before switching.
My **desk job** still ends in 2031, so the time is no guarantee.
do: **Take** evening heating and gas courses two nights a week from next September.
**Grow** savings from four to eight months by banking most of any bonus.
**Keep** the wedding but delay **children** until he has a trade.
feel: **Nervous**, but less than with two years, like changing gear before a hill.
S3.quote: I don't want my children growing up while their dad works out what he's for.
fieldNote: The extra three years mainly protect **the wedding** and let him train while still earning.
Delaying children clashes with his **family values**, and he knows it.
Sees a trade as a **bridge** until robots, not a permanent escape.

steps.text: Take evening heating and gas courses two nights a week
Bank most of the yearly bonus, aiming for eight months saved
Hold off trying for children until the trade qualification is done
Keep the accounts payable job and its pay while training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and the people who waste it have only themselves to blame. That's probably not a popular thing to say, but I believe it. I'd also say firms like Hartwell owe their staff honest notice and proper training money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I'm thirty-seven when it lands, probably with two kids and a mortgage. That's actually a worse age to be thrown out of a desk job than twenty-seven, because more people depend on you. So the extra time only helps if I use it to get out of desk work early, not to relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hartwell three or four more years and try for promotion to finance business partner, because the pay jump would help with a house. At the same time I'd do the heating courses slowly, one night a week, and work Saturdays with my uncle Michel. By thirty-two I'd want to be qualified and ready to move over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the other two, but still a low hum of worry. I'd sleep fine most nights. It's the nights after a big Hartwell announcement that I'd lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who waste the time only have themselves to blame. What about Maureen, or someone her age?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair, and I wouldn't say it about her. Someone near the end of a career who gave thirty years to one firm deserves a proper pension and a send-off, and the company should pay for it. I mean people my age, who've got the time and the health and just don't want to hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy a house in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, maybe in 2028, but a smaller one, a two-bedroom terrace rather than the three-bed semi Clara likes. We'd want a mortgage we could pay on a heating engineer's wage, not a manager's. That's the test I'd use.

say: Ten years is **a gift**, and people who waste it have themselves to blame.
Firms like Hartwell owe staff **honest notice** and proper training money.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** with kids and a mortgage, a worse age to lose a desk job.
The extra time only helps if I **leave desk work early** instead of relaxing.
do: **Try** for promotion to finance business partner within three or four years.
**Train** one night a week and work **Saturdays** with uncle Michel.
**Buy** a smaller two-bedroom terrace around 2028, sized to a tradesman's wage.
feel: Calmer, with a **low hum** of worry that flares after big Hartwell announcements.
S4.quote: We'd want a mortgage we could pay on a heating engineer's wage, not a manager's.
fieldNote: His blame for **wasted time** stops short of older workers like Maureen, who he says earned a pension.
He sees the long timeline as **more dangerous** at his life stage, because more will depend on him.
Plans every big purchase around a **tradesman's wage**, not his current salary.

steps.text: Go for promotion to finance business partner at Hartwell
Take heating courses one night a week at the college
Work Saturdays for uncle Michel's heating and plumbing firm
Buy a two-bedroom terrace around 2028 instead of a semi

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because it lands right on top of the wedding and before I've learned anything with my hands. What would help is apprenticeships that take people my age on a proper training wage, not just school leavers, and companies giving real notice instead of a Friday email. I don't want a handout, I want a fair chance to earn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what I'd tell Danny, the youngest on my team. I'd tell him to learn a trade at night while he's young and has no one depending on him. My generation was told a degree and an office job was the safe road, and I'm not sure that road goes where we were promised.

headlineQuote: My generation was told a degree and an office job was the safe road, and I'm not sure that road goes where we were promised.
portrait: Ivan Dubois, 27, runs a **seven-person accounts payable** team at a large frozen-food maker's head office.
He rents with his **fiancée Clara**, a nurse, and is saving for a June wedding and a house.
Traditional and **steady**, he trusts work, church and family, and adopts new tools once they're proven.
He sees his desk job as **highly exposed**, so faster AGI pushes him toward his uncle's heating trade.
More warning makes him **calmer** but not relaxed; he wants to use the years to leave desk work early.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it lands on the wedding before he has any hands-on skill.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** that take people his age on a proper training wage, not only school leavers.
Employers giving **real notice** instead of a Friday email.
